titles.452: Annotatio III §.IX: Form in Hoc est Corpus meum / Hic est sanguis — priest’s enunciation confects Transsubstantiation
titles.453: Annotatio III §.IX: Some require inserting causal ENIM (Matt. 26:28) under both Eucharist parts
titles.454: Annotatio III §.IX: ENIM partly aetiological, partly promissive — baptism parallel (Mark 16:16)

latin.451: §. IX. Ita habet Historia Transsubstantiationis, cujus Formam ex Magistro Sententiarum Lib. IV. Dist. VIII. c. p. m. 307. hujusque Commentatore præcipuo Thoma Aquinate, Summ. Theol. part. 3. Quæst. 78. Artic. 1. p. m. 292. reponunt.
latin.452: In Enunciatione verborum Christi: Hoc est Corpus meum, Hic est sanguis meus, vel, Hic est calix sanguinis mei, utpote quorum verborum Enuntiatione, à Sacerdote facta, Sacramentum Transsubstantiationis conficiatur.
latin.453: Contendentibus tamen nonnullis pro interferenda verbis hisce conjunctione Causativa, ENIM, quippe Matth. 26. 28. reperta, eoque nullibi non in dictis verbis utriusque partis Eucharistiæ subaudienda.
latin.454: Ceu ætiologica partim, rationem reddente, quare illud, quòd porrigebatur, edendum bibendumque fuerit, partim promissiva, quòd promissio omni Sacramento propria, in Baptismate disertis his verbis expressa legatur: Quicunque crediderit & baptizatus fuerit, salvabitur.
latin.455: Vid. Picherellum Opusc. Theol. §. 8.; Quin, tantam interferendæ dictæ voculæ conjunctivæ necessitatem opinantibus aliis, ut citra ejus adjectionem Sacramenti Formam incompletam, i. e. Transsubstantiationem haud plenè confectam dicant.
latin.456: Id quod paucis abhinc annis Reverendiss. Stillingfleedio, coram Jacobo II. M. Britanniæ Rege, cum Jesuita White, disputanti, ansam dedit monendi, Pontificiorum alios, ab aliis celebratæ scil. cum omissione particulæ Enim, Missæ, adstantes ac venerabile, quod ajunt, adorantes, non posse, vel ex propria hypothesi, ab idololatria, saltem materiali, propriè interim dicta & Israëliticæ in deserto per omnia simili, immunes manere, cùm Latriæ Cultu prosequerentur id, quod, vitio omissæ voculæ enim, nondum in verum corpus Christi transiisset.

pass_a.451: §. IX. So stands the History of Transsubstantiation, whose Form they place from the Master of the Sentences Book IV Distinction VIII chapter p. 307, and from his chief Commentator Thomas Aquinas, Summa Theol. part 3 Question 78 Article 1 p. 292.
pass_a.452: In the Enunciation of Christ’s words: This is My Body, This is My blood, or, This is the cup of My blood — inasmuch as by the Enunciation of those words, made by the Priest, the Sacrament of Transsubstantiation is confected.
pass_a.453: Some nevertheless contending for inserting into these words the Causative conjunction ENIM, found indeed at Matt. 26:28, and therefore to be understood nowhere not in the said words of either part of the Eucharist.
pass_a.454: As partly aetiological, giving the reason why that which was being offered was to be eaten and drunk, partly promissive, because the promise proper to every Sacrament is read expressed in Baptism in these express words: Whoever shall have believed and been baptized shall be saved.
pass_a.455: See Picherellus Opusc. Theol. §. 8.; Nay, others opine such necessity of inserting the said little conjunctive word that apart from its addition they call the Form of the Sacrament incomplete — i.e. Transsubstantiation not fully confected.
pass_a.456: Which a few years ago gave Most Reverend Stillingfleet, disputing before James II King of Great Britain with the Jesuit White, occasion to warn that others of the Pontificians, standing by a Mass celebrated by others namely with omission of the particle Enim, and adoring the venerable (as they say), cannot even on their own hypothesis remain immune from idolatry, at least material, properly so called and in all points like Israel’s in the desert, since by the Cult of Latria they would be pursuing that which, by fault of the omitted little word enim, had not yet passed into Christ’s true body.

451: §.IX: so the History stands; they lodge its Form in Lombard Sent. IV Dist. VIII (p. 307).
Chief commentator: Aquinas ST 3 q.78 a.1 (p. 292).
452: Form = enunciation of Christ’s words: Hoc est Corpus meum; Hic est sanguis meus; or Hic est calix sanguinis mei.
By the priest’s speaking those words, they say, the Sacrament of Transsubstantiation is confected.
453: Some insist on inserting the causative conjunction ENIM into those words.
It stands in Matt. 26:28, so they would have it understood under both Eucharist parts everywhere.
454: ENIM is partly aetiological — why what was offered was to be eaten and drunk.
Partly promissive — like Baptism’s own promise: whoever believes and is baptized shall be saved.
455: Picherellus (Opusc. Theol. §.8) is cited on this.
Others press the little word so hard that without adding ENIM they call the Form incomplete — Transsubstantiation not fully done.
456: Stillingfleet, disputing with Jesuit White before James II, used that to warn: standers at a Mass that omits Enim, adoring the ‘venerable,’ cannot escape even material idolatry on their own hypothesis.
By latria they would worship what — for want of enim — has not yet become Christ’s true body (Israel-in-the-desert parallel).
Stop before §.X (Transsubstantiation unworthy of Christ’s banquet; eliminate from the Church).
